newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel list doubts about new Czech economic plan.
newsitem.headline: Havel list doubts about new Czech economic plan.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel cast a pall over the ruling coalition's latest economic recovery programme on Thursday, saying he had doubts about its long-term aims and the accompanying ministerial changes.
In a statement issued by his office, Havel said the programme could possibly resolve the immediate situation but did not address government plans for the longer term.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his two junior coalition partners agreed on Wednesday to unspecified budget cuts, public sector wage freezes and ministerial changes to restore confidence in the crown, the economy and the government.
Havel said he expressed several doubts about the programme at a meeting with the three coalition leaders but he indicated he might confirm the cabinet changes next Monday.

He said the programme "still does not mention even a word about long-term programme aims of this coalition and government, and does not, in the new situation, develop and make concrete its programme statement."
He said it did not say "even a word" of who was responsible for the economic crisis and he could not understand the connection between the personnel changes and the new programme.

The agreement followed two weeks of speculative pressure on the Czech crown. The Czech National Bank (CNB) was forced to allow the currency to float, sparking a further eight percent drop in its value.
The crown firmed against the mark in morning trade to stand at 19.138 to the mark and 32.575 to the dollar at 1130 GMT, compared with 19.306 and 32.737 late on Wednesday.
"The crown reacted positively to the changes in the government and the newly-announced plan," said trader Jan Dosek of CSOB.

"Everything they want to do is great. I just give them about a five percent chance of actually being able to execute it and that is what the market is sceptical about," said Matt Starr, director of capital markets at Creditanstalt in Prague.
Klaus, a confident monetarist economist who took personal credit for the post-communist economic transformation, admitted on Wednesday that mistakes were made during his five years in charge.
He said the recovery programme, following an earlier set of measures in April, would be painful but was the fastest way to restore growth.
In the meantime, he said, the price would be higher inflation, more unemployment, lower wages and a fall in output.
Education Minister Ivan Pilip, seen as part of Klaus's inner circle, is to take over as finance minister for Ivan Kocarnik, blamed by many Czechs for the worsening economic situation.
The Czech ambassador to Britain, Karel Kuhnl, will be the new trade and industry minister.
